lessons.title: What is cloud computing?
lessons.summary: Cloud computing delivers computing resources as services so organizations can create and release capacity without owning every layer of infrastructure.
learningObjectives: Describe cloud computing as on-demand compute, storage, networking, and platforms
Identify how cloud services reduce fixed hardware ownership
Recognize scenarios where rapid capacity and provider infrastructure are benefits
lessons.explanation:
**What is cloud computing?** is part of the AZ-900 cloud concepts domain. It explains how compute, storage, networking, and platforms can be consumed as services rather than purchased as fixed hardware. Cloud learning at this level is about reasoning from the business requirement to the right model, benefit, or responsibility split. A cloud provider operates large-scale infrastructure and exposes services that customers can use without buying every physical component themselves. The customer still owns business decisions such as data classification, user access, secure configuration, monitoring, and cost awareness.

For beginners, focus on the vocabulary in the scenario. If a requirement mentions rapid provisioning, short-lived environments, or variable demand, think about cloud characteristics such as on-demand access and elasticity. If it mentions who protects data or assigns permissions, think about the shared responsibility model. If it mentions public, private, or hybrid, identify whether resources are provider-operated, dedicated to one organization, or combined across environments.

Cloud advantages are strongest when teams design and operate carefully. High availability, reliability, scalability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability are capabilities to use, not automatic outcomes. Teams should choose appropriate services, configure access, apply standards, monitor usage, and revise designs as needs change. That practical reasoning is more important than memorizing isolated product names.
lessons.businessScenario: Fabrikam Training runs evening workshops for students. Instead of buying servers for occasional registration spikes, the team wants temporary computing power, storage, and networking that can be provisioned from Azure when classes open and reduced when enrolment closes.
lessons.technicalExample: For a short pilot, the team creates a resource group, deploys a small web app and database, assigns access to the course administrators, and monitors use. The important idea is not a specific service name; it is that compute, storage, and networking are delivered as services over the internet rather than purchased as fixed hardware.

misconception.myth: Cloud computing is simply someone else's computer with no meaningful choices for the customer.
misconception.reality: Azure supplies shared datacenters and managed services, but customers still choose regions, service types, access controls, data protection settings, and cost controls for their workloads.

lessons.examTakeaway: When a scenario emphasizes rapid provisioning, internet-accessible services, measured usage, or avoiding hardware purchases, connect it to the basic definition of cloud computing.
lessons.recap: Cloud computing means delivering technology services such as compute, storage, and networking over the internet with self-service provisioning and usage-based consumption. You gain speed and flexibility, but you still design, secure, and govern what you deploy.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of cloud computing like using a city bike scheme. You do not buy and maintain every bicycle; you unlock one when needed, ride it, and return it. You still choose the route, follow the rules, and look after anything you carry.
lessons.anotherExample: A community theatre sells tickets online for only a few shows each month. Azure lets it host the ticket site during sale periods without buying permanent servers that sit idle between events.

data.title: Definition clue
data.body: Look for words such as *on demand*, *over the internet*, *shared pool of resources*, and *pay for what you use*. Those clues point to cloud computing fundamentals rather than to one specific Azure product.

flashcards.back: Delivery of computing services such as servers, storage, databases, networking, and software over the internet.
Creating or scaling resources when they are needed instead of waiting for new physical hardware.
Cloud services can track consumption so organizations can align cost with actual use.
Customers still choose configuration, access, data protection, governance, and cost controls.

tr.title: Cloud computing nedir?
tr.summary: Cloud computing, kuruluşların altyapının her katmanına sahip olmadan kaynak oluşturup bırakabilmesi için bilişim kaynaklarını hizmet olarak sunar.
learningObjectives: Cloud computing kavramını isteğe bağlı compute, storage, networking ve platformlar olarak açıkla
Cloud hizmetlerinin sabit donanım sahipliğini nasıl azalttığını belirle
Hızlı kapasite ve sağlayıcı altyapısının fayda olduğu senaryoları tanı
tr.explanation: **Cloud computing**, işlem, depolama, ağ ve platform yeteneklerinin bir ağ üzerinden hizmet olarak sunulmasıdır. Kuruluşlar her fiziksel bileşeni satın almak yerine ihtiyaç duyduklarında kaynak ister, kullanır ve gerekmediğinde bırakır. Bu yaklaşım özellikle pilot çalışmalar, kısa süreli test ortamları ve değişken talep için yararlıdır. Cloud sağlayıcısı büyük ölçekli altyapıyı işletir; müşteri ise veri, kimlik, erişim, güvenli yapılandırma, izleme ve maliyet farkındalığı gibi iş kararlarından sorumlu kalır.
tr.businessScenario: Fabrikam Training akşam atölyeleri düzenler. Kayıt dönemlerindeki kısa yoğunluklar için sunucu satın almak yerine ekip, dersler açıldığında Azure’dan geçici işlem gücü, depolama ve ağ kaynakları sağlamayı, kayıtlar kapanınca da bunları azaltmayı ister.
tr.technicalExample: Kısa bir pilot için ekip bir resource group oluşturur, küçük bir web uygulaması ve veritabanı dağıtır, kurs yöneticilerine erişim verir ve kullanımı izler. Önemli fikir belirli bir hizmet adı değil; işlem, depolama ve ağın sabit donanım satın almak yerine internet üzerinden hizmet olarak sunulmasıdır.

misconception.myth: Bulut bilişim, müşterinin anlamlı seçim yapmadığı şekilde yalnızca başkasının bilgisayarını kullanmaktır.
misconception.reality: Azure paylaşılan veri merkezleri ve yönetilen hizmetler sağlar; ancak müşteriler iş yükleri için bölgeyi, hizmet türünü, erişim denetimlerini, veri koruma ayarlarını ve maliyet kontrollerini yine seçer.

tr.examTakeaway: Bir senaryo hızlı kaynak sağlama, internet üzerinden erişilen hizmetler, ölçülen kullanım veya donanım satın almaktan kaçınma vurgusu yapıyorsa bunu bulut bilişimin temel tanımıyla ilişkilendirin.
tr.recap: Bulut bilişim; işlem, depolama ve ağ gibi teknoloji hizmetlerinin internet üzerinden, self servis kaynak sağlama ve kullanıma dayalı tüketimle sunulmasıdır. Hız ve esneklik kazanırsınız; ancak dağıttığınız şeyleri tasarlama, güvenliğini sağlama ve yönetme sorumluluğunuz devam eder.
tr.simplerExplanation: Bulut bilişimi şehir bisikleti sistemi gibi düşünün. Her bisikleti satın alıp bakımını yapmazsınız; gerektiğinde birini açar, kullanır ve geri bırakırsınız. Yine de rotayı siz seçer, kurallara uyar ve yanınızdaki eşyadan siz sorumlu olursunuz.
tr.anotherExample: Bir mahalle tiyatrosu ayda yalnızca birkaç gösteri için çevrimiçi bilet satar. Azure, gösteriler arasında boşta kalacak kalıcı sunucular satın almadan bilet sitesini satış dönemlerinde barındırmasını sağlar.

extraBlocks.title: Tanım ipucu
extraBlocks.body: *İsteğe bağlı*, *internet üzerinden*, *paylaşılan kaynak havuzu* ve *kullandığın kadar öde* gibi ifadeleri arayın. Bu ipuçları tek bir Azure ürününden çok bulut bilişimin temellerini gösterir.

flashcards.back: Sunucu, depolama, veritabanı, ağ ve yazılım gibi bilişim hizmetlerinin internet üzerinden sunulması.
Yeni fiziksel donanımı beklemek yerine kaynakları ihtiyaç duyulduğunda oluşturmak veya ölçeklendirmek.
Bulut hizmetleri tüketimi izleyebilir; böylece kuruluşlar maliyeti gerçek kullanımla ilişkilendirebilir.
Yapılandırma, erişim, veri koruma, yönetişim ve maliyet kontrollerini müşteri seçmeye devam eder.

lessons.title: The shared responsibility model
lessons.summary: Explains which cloud tasks belong to the provider, which remain with the customer, and how the split changes by service type.
learningObjectives: Explain which responsibilities stay with the customer in cloud services
Distinguish provider and customer duties across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
Recognize why data, access, and business configuration remain customer responsibilities
lessons.explanation:
**The shared responsibility model** is part of the AZ-900 cloud concepts domain. It clarifies that cloud adoption shifts some operational work to the provider without transferring ownership of customer data or access choices. Cloud learning at this level is about reasoning from the business requirement to the right model, benefit, or responsibility split. A cloud provider operates large-scale infrastructure and exposes services that customers can use without buying every physical component themselves. The customer still owns business decisions such as data classification, user access, secure configuration, monitoring, and cost awareness.

For beginners, focus on the vocabulary in the scenario. If a requirement mentions rapid provisioning, short-lived environments, or variable demand, think about cloud characteristics such as on-demand access and elasticity. If it mentions who protects data or assigns permissions, think about the shared responsibility model. If it mentions public, private, or hybrid, identify whether resources are provider-operated, dedicated to one organization, or combined across environments.

Cloud advantages are strongest when teams design and operate carefully. High availability, reliability, scalability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability are capabilities to use, not automatic outcomes. Teams should choose appropriate services, configure access, apply standards, monitor usage, and revise designs as needs change. That practical reasoning is more important than memorizing isolated product names.

terminology.definition: Division of duties between provider and customer.
Data, identity, access, and configuration tasks.

lessons.businessScenario: Woodgrove Bank is moving a staff scheduling app to Azure. Leaders need to know which tasks Microsoft handles for the cloud platform and which tasks remain with Woodgrove, especially user access, data classification, and application configuration.
lessons.technicalExample: If Woodgrove runs a virtual machine, Microsoft operates the physical datacenter and host infrastructure, while Woodgrove patches the guest operating system, manages the app, and controls identities. If Woodgrove uses SaaS, the provider manages more of the stack, but Woodgrove still controls users, data, and business settings.

misconception.myth: The shared responsibility model is a fixed checklist that never changes between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
misconception.reality: Responsibility shifts by service type. The provider always runs the cloud infrastructure, but customers always retain responsibility for their data, identities, and decisions about access.

lessons.examTakeaway: Watch for the service type. IaaS leaves more operating-system and application work with the customer; SaaS shifts most platform operation to the provider, while customer data and access decisions remain customer responsibilities.
lessons.recap: Shared responsibility explains who manages each layer of a cloud solution. Moving up from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS usually reduces customer operational tasks, but it does not remove responsibility for data, identities, permissions, and business configuration.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of a hotel. The hotel maintains the building, lifts, and utilities. You still lock your room, decide who gets a key card, and look after your own belongings.
lessons.anotherExample: A school using Microsoft 365 does not patch the mail servers, but it still decides which staff accounts exist, which groups can access files, and how sensitive student data is handled.

columns.title: More provider-managed
points: Customer still manages data and access

data.title: Service-type clue
data.body: For shared responsibility questions, first identify whether the scenario is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS. Then ask: is this about the physical cloud platform, or about the customer's data, identities, app settings, and access?

flashcards.back: A way to describe which security and operational tasks belong to the cloud provider and which remain with the customer.

The provider manages physical infrastructure; the customer manages the guest OS, applications, data, and access.
The provider manages most infrastructure and application operation; the customer manages users, data, and configuration.

tr.title: Paylaşılan sorumluluk modeli
tr.summary: Paylaşılan sorumluluk modeli, hangi cloud görevlerinin sağlayıcıya, hangilerinin müşteriye ait olduğunu ve hizmet türüne göre bu dağılımın nasıl değiştiğini açıklar.
learningObjectives: Cloud hizmetlerinde hangi sorumlulukların müşteride kaldığını açıkla
IaaS, PaaS ve SaaS arasında sağlayıcı ve müşteri görevlerini ayırt et
Veri, erişim ve iş yapılandırmasının neden müşteride kaldığını tanı
tr.explanation: **Paylaşılan sorumluluk modeli**, cloud sağlayıcısı ile müşteri arasındaki görev paylaşımını açıklar. Sağlayıcı fiziksel tesisleri, donanımı ve provider-managed altyapıyı işletir. Müşteri ise kendi verisini, kimliklerini, erişim kararlarını, yapılandırmalarını ve iş yükünün kullanımını yönetmeye devam eder. IaaS daha fazla müşteri kontrolü ve işletim işi bırakır; PaaS platform işlerinin daha fazlasını sağlayıcıya aktarır; SaaS uygulama yığınının çoğunu sağlayıcıya bırakır. Ancak SaaS kullanırken bile kullanıcılar, veri ve uygun kullanım müşterinin sorumluluğundadır.

terminology.definition: Görevlerin sağlayıcı ve müşteri arasında bölünmesi.
Veri, kimlik, erişim ve yapılandırma gibi müşteride kalan görevler.
Fiziksel tesisler ve sağlayıcı altyapısı gibi sağlayıcının yönettiği görevler.

tr.businessScenario: Woodgrove Bank personel planlama uygulamasını Azure’a taşıyor. Yöneticiler özellikle kullanıcı erişimi, veri sınıflandırması ve uygulama yapılandırması için Microsoft’un bulut platformunda hangi görevleri üstlendiğini, hangilerinin Woodgrove’da kaldığını bilmek istiyor.
tr.technicalExample: Woodgrove bir sanal makine çalıştırırsa Microsoft fiziksel veri merkezini ve ana altyapıyı işletir; Woodgrove ise konuk işletim sistemine yama uygular, uygulamayı yönetir ve kimlikleri denetler. Woodgrove SaaS kullanırsa sağlayıcı yığının daha büyük bölümünü yönetir; ancak kullanıcılar, veriler ve iş ayarları yine Woodgrove’un denetimindedir.

misconception.myth: Paylaşılan sorumluluk modeli IaaS, PaaS ve SaaS arasında hiç değişmeyen sabit bir listedir.
misconception.reality: Sorumluluk hizmet türüne göre değişir. Sağlayıcı her zaman bulut altyapısını işletir; müşteri ise verileri, kimlikleri ve erişim kararları üzerindeki sorumluluğu her zaman korur.

tr.examTakeaway: Hizmet türüne dikkat edin. IaaS, işletim sistemi ve uygulama işleri açısından müşteriye daha fazla görev bırakır; SaaS platform işletiminin çoğunu sağlayıcıya devreder, ancak müşteri verileri ve erişim kararları müşteride kalır.
tr.recap: Paylaşılan sorumluluk, bulut çözümündeki her katmanı kimin yönettiğini açıklar. IaaS’tan PaaS’a ve SaaS’a ilerledikçe müşteri operasyon görevleri genellikle azalır; ancak veri, kimlik, izin ve iş yapılandırması sorumluluğu ortadan kalkmaz.
tr.simplerExplanation: Bunu bir otel gibi düşünün. Otel binayı, asansörleri ve altyapıyı korur. Siz yine de odanızı kilitler, kime kart verileceğine karar verir ve kendi eşyalarınızdan sorumlu olursunuz.
tr.anotherExample: Microsoft 365 kullanan bir okul posta sunucularına yama uygulamaz; ancak hangi personel hesaplarının var olacağına, hangi grupların dosyalara erişeceğine ve hassas öğrenci verilerinin nasıl işleneceğine yine kendisi karar verir.

lessons.title: Public, private, and hybrid cloud
lessons.summary: Public, private, and hybrid cloud models describe how cloud environments are deployed and combined.
learningObjectives: Distinguish provider-hosted, dedicated, and connected cloud environments
Choose a deployment model from dedicated, provider-hosted, or connected-environment clues
Recognize how hybrid cloud combines Azure with private or on-premises systems
lessons.explanation:
**Public, private, and hybrid cloud** is part of the AZ-900 cloud concepts domain. It compares provider-operated public cloud, dedicated private cloud, and combinations that connect cloud with private or on-premises environments. Cloud learning at this level is about reasoning from the business requirement to the right model, benefit, or responsibility split. A cloud provider operates large-scale infrastructure and exposes services that customers can use without buying every physical component themselves. The customer still owns business decisions such as data classification, user access, secure configuration, monitoring, and cost awareness.

For beginners, focus on the vocabulary in the scenario. If a requirement mentions rapid provisioning, short-lived environments, or variable demand, think about cloud characteristics such as on-demand access and elasticity. If it mentions who protects data or assigns permissions, think about the shared responsibility model. lessons.businessScenario: Northwind Traders has a public website, a factory system that must stay in its own datacenter, and a reporting workload that needs data from both. The architecture discussion is about choosing public cloud, private cloud, or a hybrid approach for each part.
lessons.technicalExample: The public site can run in Azure public cloud. The factory control system can remain in a private environment. A secure connection can support a hybrid reporting flow that reads approved data from both locations.

misconception.myth: Hybrid cloud means a company has failed to move fully to Azure.
misconception.reality: Hybrid cloud is a valid design when regulatory, latency, legacy, or business requirements require some resources to stay outside the public cloud while other workloads use Azure.

lessons.examTakeaway: Map the requirement to the deployment model: public for provider-operated shared cloud resources, private for dedicated environments, and hybrid when a scenario connects both.
lessons.recap: Public, private, and hybrid cloud describe where resources run and who can use the environment. The best model depends on isolation, control, compliance, connectivity, and modernization goals.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Imagine event venues. A public cloud is like renting space in a large conference center, a private cloud is your own company auditorium, and hybrid is using both with a shuttle between them.
lessons.anotherExample: A hospital can keep a specialist imaging system in its own facility while using Azure for appointment reminders and analytics dashboards that do not require the device to move.

lessons.title: Consumption-based pricing and serverless
lessons.summary: Consumption-based pricing and serverless help teams align resource use with demand while reducing idle infrastructure management.
learningObjectives: Explain how consumption-based pricing charges for measured use
Describe serverless as code execution without managing servers directly
Choose serverless for intermittent event-driven workloads
lessons.explanation:
**Consumption-based pricing and serverless** is part of the AZ-900 cloud concepts domain. It distinguishes paying based on use from buying fixed capacity and explains that serverless abstracts server management but still uses servers. Cloud learning at this level is about reasoning from the business requirement to the right model, benefit, or responsibility split. A cloud provider operates large-scale infrastructure and exposes services that customers can use without buying every physical component themselves. The customer still owns business decisions such as data classification, user access, secure configuration, monitoring, and cost awareness.

For beginners, focus on the vocabulary in the scenario. If a requirement mentions rapid provisioning, short-lived environments, or variable demand, think about cloud characteristics such as on-demand access and elasticity. If it mentions who protects data or assigns permissions, think about the shared responsibility model. If it mentions public, private, or hybrid, identify whether resources are provider-operated, dedicated to one organization, or combined across environments.

Cloud advantages are strongest when teams design and operate carefully. High availability, reliability, scalability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability are capabilities to use, not automatic outcomes. Teams should choose appropriate services, configure access, apply standards, monitor usage, and revise designs as needs change. That practical reasoning is more important than memorizing isolated product names.

terminology.definition: Resources available but not doing useful work.

lessons.businessScenario: Litware Finance processes expense receipts at the end of each month. The workload is quiet most days, then runs heavily for a short period. The team wants a model that avoids paying for idle capacity where possible.
lessons.technicalExample: The team compares a continuously running VM with an event-driven function that starts when receipts arrive. Consumption-based pricing aligns better with intermittent work, while serverless reduces the need to manage servers for that processing step.

misconception.myth: Serverless means there are no servers and therefore no architecture decisions.
misconception.reality: Servers still exist, but the provider abstracts much of their management. You still design triggers, permissions, monitoring, data flow, and cost controls.

lessons.examTakeaway: For bursty or event-driven work, look for consumption and serverless clues. For steady workloads that need full OS control, a VM may still be the better fit.
lessons.recap: Consumption-based models charge according to usage rather than a fixed hardware purchase. Serverless services can run code or workflows without customer-managed servers, which is useful for event-driven and variable workloads.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of electricity in a meeting room. You switch the lights on when people arrive and off when they leave; you do not buy a generator that runs all month for one monthly meeting.
lessons.anotherExample: A sports club uploads match photos on weekends. A serverless process can create thumbnails when images arrive instead of running a full-time image server all week.

data.title: Usage-pattern clue

lessons.title: Benefits of cloud services
lessons.summary: Cloud services can improve availability, scalability, reliability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability when used well.
learningObjectives: Identify cloud benefits such as scalability, reliability, security, governance, and manageability
Match availability, demand, recovery, and standards clues to cloud benefits
Explain how cloud controls support predictable operations
lessons.explanation:
**Benefits of cloud services** is part of the AZ-900 cloud concepts domain. It maps common benefits to scenario clues such as uptime, changing demand, recovery, standards, security controls, and operational tooling. Cloud learning at this level is about reasoning from the business requirement to the right model, benefit, or responsibility split. A cloud provider operates large-scale infrastructure and exposes services that customers can use without buying every physical component themselves. The customer still owns business decisions such as data classification, user access, secure configuration, monitoring, and cost awareness.

For beginners, focus on the vocabulary in the scenario. If a requirement mentions rapid provisioning, short-lived environments, or variable demand, think about cloud characteristics such as on-demand access and elasticity. If it mentions who protects data or assigns permissions, think about the shared responsibility model. If it mentions public, private, or hybrid, identify whether resources are provider-operated, dedicated to one organization, or combined across environments.

Cloud advantages are strongest when teams design and operate carefully. High availability, reliability, scalability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability are capabilities to use, not automatic outcomes. Teams should choose appropriate services, configure access, apply standards, monitor usage, and revise designs as needs change. That practical reasoning is more important than memorizing isolated product names.

terminology.definition: Standards and controls for cloud use.

lessons.businessScenario: Proseware Learning expects unpredictable traffic when a new training course launches. The team wants the site to stay available, scale for demand, apply consistent security rules, and remain manageable by a small operations group.
lessons.technicalExample: The design uses scalable hosting, health monitoring, backup and recovery planning, access controls, and policy-based governance. Each feature supports a different cloud benefit: scalability, reliability, security, governance, and manageability.

misconception.myth: High availability, scalability, reliability, and manageability all mean the same thing.
misconception.reality: They are related but different. Availability is about being reachable, scalability is about handling demand changes, reliability is about recovering from failure, and manageability is about operating the environment effectively.

lessons.examTakeaway: Read the problem statement for the benefit being requested: demand changes suggest scalability, outage tolerance suggests reliability or availability, standards suggest governance, and easier operations suggest manageability.
lessons.recap: Azure benefits are most useful when you can match each term to a business need. Cloud services can help scale, recover, secure, govern, and manage workloads, but each benefit requires deliberate design choices.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of a popular café. More tables handle a rush (scalability), spare equipment helps when a coffee machine fails (reliability), opening hours keep service reachable (availability), and a checklist helps staff run shifts consistently (manageability).
lessons.anotherExample: A charity donation site can scale during a campaign, use monitoring to detect issues, apply access policies for volunteers, and review recommendations to improve operations after the event.

data.title: Benefit wording

lessons.title: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
lessons.summary: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS describe how much of the technology stack the provider manages and how much remains with the customer.
learningObjectives: Compare IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS by stack management and customer control
Choose IaaS for OS control, PaaS for custom code, or SaaS for ready-to-use apps
Explain how responsibility decreases as services move from IaaS to SaaS
lessons.explanation:
**IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS** is part of the AZ-900 cloud concepts domain. It compares control and responsibility: IaaS offers more control, PaaS supports custom code on a managed platform, and SaaS is ready-to-use software. Cloud learning at this level is about reasoning from the business requirement to the right model, benefit, or responsibility split. A cloud provider operates large-scale infrastructure and exposes services that customers can use without buying every physical component themselves. The customer still owns business decisions such as data classification, user access, secure configuration, monitoring, and cost awareness.

For beginners, focus on the vocabulary in the scenario. If a requirement mentions rapid provisioning, short-lived environments, or variable demand, think about cloud characteristics such as on-demand access and elasticity. If it mentions who protects data or assigns permissions, think about the shared responsibility model. If it mentions public, private, or hybrid, identify whether resources are provider-operated, dedicated to one organization, or combined across environments.

Cloud advantages are strongest when teams design and operate carefully. High availability, reliability, scalability, predictability, security, governance, and manageability are capabilities to use, not automatic outcomes. Teams should choose appropriate services, configure access, apply standards, monitor usage, and revise designs as needs change. That practical reasoning is more important than memorizing isolated product names.

terminology.definition: Infrastructure as a service with more customer control.
Ready-to-use application delivered as a service.

lessons.businessScenario: Adventure Works is modernizing three systems: a legacy payroll app that needs custom OS settings, a new web API where developers want to focus on code, and a collaboration tool for employees. The team must choose IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS for each need.
lessons.technicalExample: A virtual machine can support the legacy app because it offers OS control. Azure App Service or another platform service can host the API with less infrastructure work. A SaaS collaboration app provides ready-to-use functionality with minimal customer management.

misconception.myth: SaaS is always better than PaaS, and PaaS is always better than IaaS.
misconception.reality: The best service type depends on control, customization, management effort, and business fit. IaaS can be appropriate when OS control is required; SaaS is best when the ready-made app meets the need.

lessons.examTakeaway: Use control and management clues. Need guest OS control: IaaS. Need to deploy custom code without managing servers: PaaS. Need a ready-to-use application: SaaS.
lessons.recap: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS describe how much of the stack the provider manages. As you move from IaaS to SaaS, customer infrastructure work generally decreases while provider management increases.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think about meals. IaaS is renting a kitchen and cooking everything yourself, PaaS is using a meal kit with the hard prep done, and SaaS is ordering a finished meal.
lessons.anotherExample: A developer team might run a test domain controller on a VM, publish a customer portal on a platform service, and use a hosted CRM system for sales staff.

columns.title: More provider-managed
points: Customer still manages data and access

data.title: Service type shortcut
data.body: Ask what the customer wants to manage. More control usually points to IaaS. Less infrastructure management for custom apps points to PaaS. Ready-made business capability points to SaaS.

flashcards.back: Infrastructure as a service: customer manages the OS, applications, data, and access on provider-managed infrastructure.
Platform as a service: customer deploys apps and data while the provider manages much of the platform.
Software as a service: customer uses a ready-made application and manages users, data, and configuration.
Choose based on required control, customization, and how much management the customer wants to keep.
